evidence.quote: I've struggled a lot with my art process being slower than I'd like it to be. It doesn't feel great to reach the end of a time constraint and know that there's so much more you wanted to do but weren't efficient enough to fit in. I've started doing some things for both my rendered and line illustrations that have really helped me add a lot more detail without it taking a ton of time, and its made my quicker work start to look quite a bit more finished than it used to.

There are some unique challenges and things to keep in mind when you're animating something like a chase or fight sequence. It's really important that you can make an action look fast and bold enough, or the strike of a weapon impactful enough. I think learning how to do this well is a great way to improve your animation skills quickly, since it requires you to practice the things that beginner animators tend to struggle with or get wrong.

I've noticed that the people who watch these videos seem to really like doing things as fast as possible, so here's 7 tips I have to make your drawing process more efficient. It's something I've been working on getting better at myself, and this is everything that has helped me.

Lighting can do a lot to take an animation from looking just good to really impressive and cinematic, but especially if you're working in a limited program, figuring out how to manage that might not seem very straightforward. Luckily, it can be made much easier with some easy-to-use tricks, and a lot of these dont require anything other than ideally the ability to seperate different parts of your animation into layers.

A great solution to the common feeling that your lineart looks worse than your rougher sketch is texture. When drawing something, you may be focused on outlining each main object, but the result will tend to look flat and plain in most styles. The detail inside of objects is often not pushed far enough, or neglected entirely. By detailing not just the outer edges of a subject but the inside as well, you end up with something that looks much more tangable and interesting.

Timing charts can be pretty confusing for anyone getting into 2d animation. There are some good resources out there about how to use them, but not as many explaining what their usefulness is, and who should actually be using them. You might be unsure if you're supposed to or would benefit from creating timing charts for your own animations. That is what I'll mostly focus on here, but first I'll explain briefly what they're for and how they work.
